description: We're Darb (Arabic for "path"), a team of high school friends from Ramallah working on the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. We build fast using AI tools to turn ideas into an interactive map that helps astronauts plan a safe Marswalk using NASA data. This team is for friends only.
summary: Darb ("path" in Arabic) helps an astronaut plan a safe walk on Mars. We chose lower Mount Sharp in Gale Crater, where NASA's Curiosity rover studied boxwork ridges in 2025, and set a science goal: walk there and collect samples. Darb layers real NASA data — 1-metre HiRISE elevation, CTX and Viking imagery, THEMIS night-time infrared (rock vs. loose sand), CRISM minerals, Curiosity's REMS weather, RAD radiation and Navcam photos — into one walking-scale map. Click a start and a goal: an A* path-finder avoids steep slopes, rough ground and sand, and reports distance, walking time, oxygen reserve, radiation dose and a 🟢/🟡/🔴 safety score. A helmet HUD, buddy mode for two astronauts and real rover photos at each stop help the crew know what to expect. Because a message to Earth takes 4–24 minutes, our AI assistant "Ask Darb" runs on the device with no internet, answers only from the map's data and says "I don't know" otherwise (54/54 on our test set). It matters because the first Mars walkers will need mission-control-quality planning without mission control.
details:
What it does

  • A Mars map of lower Mount Sharp with 6 toggleable layers: terrain slope (HiRISE 1 m elevation, 25 m cells), rough ground (rocks and small ridges, from the same 1 m data), thermal-inertia proxy (THEMIS night IR), minerals (CRISM), elevation hillshade (MOLA), and Curiosity's real traverse with 8 stops from its 2025 boxwork campaign.
  • Route planner: click START and GOAL → the safest walking route appears as a dotted trail. A point clicked on too-steep ground is moved to the nearest walkable spot within 150 m.
  • Route card: distance, one-way and round-trip time, O₂ reserve after return, climb/descent, max slope, % loose sand, % very rough ground, radiation dose, and a safety score with reasons.
  • Waypoints: a real Curiosity Navcam photo from each stop, with what to look for (boxwork ridges 1–2 m tall, central fractures, sandy hollows).
  • Weather and radiation panel: latest REMS sol and RAD surface dose.
  • HUD mode: helmet-visor view with compass, distance to goal, O₂ timer, slope, today's Earth light-delay and warnings.
  • Buddy mode: a route wide enough for two astronauts who must stay within a chosen distance of each other.
  • Ask Darb: an offline AI assistant (English or Arabic) for questions like "Is this route safe?", "What minerals are near waypoint 3?" or "Explain the rock photo at waypoint 6" (a local vision model looks at the real photo).
  • A guided 10-step tour for presenting, and an English/Arabic interface.

How it works

  1. A Python script (standard library only) downloads and prepares real data: the USGS 1 m HiRISE elevation model of Gale Crater (a 3.87 GB file, read with our own TIFF reader), THEMIS tiles, CRISM mineral maps, REMS weather and Curiosity's positions and photos. It builds a grid of 515 × 560 cells (~25 m) with elevation, slope, roughness (height steps over 4 m inside each cell) and a thermal value.
  2. Each cell gets a cost: steeper, rougher or sandier costs more; steeper than 20° is blocked.
  3. A* finds the lowest-cost path in a few milliseconds. Walking time uses a hiking formula scaled so flat ground = 2 km/h for a suited astronaut; oxygen use assumes an 8-hour life-support budget for the round trip.
  4. Ask Darb (Ollama, local open model qwen3.5:9b) receives the current facts in plain English with a strict rule to use only those facts. The safety score itself is computed by our algorithm, not by the AI.
  5. Map tiles for the study area are stored on the device: a full demo makes zero internet requests.

What we measured

  • Demo route (Curiosity's 2024 site → its 2025 boxwork stop): 2.73 km, 1 h 38 min one way, 61 % O₂ reserve, max slope 10.5°, 🟡 Caution. With buddy mode at 100 m the two astronauts can't fit through the narrow safe gaps: a 5.29 km detour, 🔴 Danger.
  • Our elevation matched Curiosity's own recorded elevation within 4.2 m at its 8 stops in 2025, and an independent model using ESA Mars Express HRSC data: average bias +3.7 m, typical (median absolute) difference 12.1 m.
  • Ask Darb test set: 18 questions (12 facts, 6 with no answer in the data) × 3 runs = 54/54 correct, 1.9 s per answer.
  • 20 automated unit tests for the route planner pass.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve

  • One walking-scale view of the safety-critical data (slope, roughness, sand, oxygen time, radiation, weather) instead of separate regional maps.
  • Shows that a useful, tested AI assistant can work with no link to Earth.
  • Every number is traceable to a cited NASA source, and the limits are stated openly (e.g. single boulders are smaller than a 25 m cell; the slope limits and 2 km/h speed are our assumptions).
  • Bilingual (English/Arabic) to bring Mars exploration data to more students.

Tools, coding languages, hardware and software

HTML, CSS, JavaScript (Leaflet.js 1.9.4); Python 3 (data preparation, standard library only); Node.js test runner; Ollama with local open models (qwen3.5:9b; gpt-oss:20b for comparison); Git. Developed and tested on a Windows 11 PC (Intel i7-14700F, 32 GB RAM, NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB). AI assistance in development is described in the "Use of Super Intelligence" field and in AI-USAGE.md in the repository.
